cards.explanation: Job's one big wish is to know where to find God. He says, “If only I knew where to find Him, so that I could go to His seat.” (Job 23:3) He's hurting, and his biggest wish is still to find God. I think that tells you where Job's heart is pointing. When life gets heavy, he wants to go to God's seat.

The answer is False. Job wants more than a speech. He says, “I would learn how He would answer, and consider what He would say.” (Job 23:5) He's ready to listen, friends, which tells you he wants an actual answer and not just a chance to vent.

Job says God would certainly take note of him. He says, “No, He would certainly take note of me.” (Job 23:6) Job wonders if God would contend with him in great power, and then he answers his own question. He believes God would pay attention to him. That's a lot of hope from a man in this much pain.

The word is “delivered.” Job says, “…I would be delivered forever from my Judge.” (Job 23:7) He calls God his Judge here. He pictures an upright man reasoning with Him and walking away set free. That's the outcome Job is hoping for.

What God knows is the way Job has taken. Job says, “Yet He knows the way I have taken…” (Job 23:10) He can't see God anywhere, but he's sure God sees him. That one little “yet” carries a lot of weight, friends. I think Job is holding on to it.
The word is “gold.” Job says, “when He has tested me, I will come forth as gold.” (Job 23:10) He expects to come out as gold after God has tested him. That's a bold thing for a hurting man to say.

Job says he has not departed from the command of God's lips. His words are, “I have not departed from the command of His lips…” (Job 23:12) Then he adds that he has treasured the words of God's mouth more than his daily bread. For a man this hungry for answers, that's a big claim. God's words come first, even before bread.

The answer is True. Job says, “For He carries out His decree against me, and He has many such plans.” (Job 23:14) The mood is heavy here. Job feels that what he's facing may not be the only thing God has planned. It's no wonder fear comes next.

The word is “terrified.” Job says, “Therefore I am terrified in His presence; when I consider this, I fear Him.” (Job 23:15) He just said God is unchangeable and does what He desires. Thinking it over, Job is afraid. He says it plainly, with no sugarcoating.

The answer is False. Job says, “Yet I am not silenced by the darkness, by the thick darkness that covers my face.” (Job 23:17) His heart is faint and he's afraid, but he keeps talking. That little “yet” shows up again, friends.
First on Job's list is moving boundary stones. He says, “Men move boundary stones; they pasture stolen flocks.” (Job 24:2) Moving boundary stones comes first. Stolen flocks come right behind it.

The answer is True. Job says, “They push the needy off the road and force all the poor of the land into hiding.” (Job 24:4) The poor aren't just struggling. They're being pushed out of sight. Job is laying out what he sees.

The poor huddle against the rocks. Job says, “Drenched by mountain rains, they huddle against the rocks for want of shelter.” (Job 24:8) No roof, so a rock is the wall they've got. I think this one hurts to picture.

For all that work, the poor still go hungry and thirsty. Job says, “They carry the sheaves, but still go hungry.” (Job 24:10) Then he says they tread the winepresses, “…but go thirsty.” (Job 24:11) They do the work, and the harvest doesn't feed them. I think this one is heavy, friends, and it's okay to feel it.

The answer is “no one.” Job says, “From the city, men groan, and the souls of the wounded cry out, yet God charges no one with wrongdoing.” (Job 24:12) The cries are loud, and Job doesn't see anyone being charged. That's his complaint.

Job says the murderer is like a thief in the night. His words are, “When daylight is gone, the murderer rises to kill the poor and needy; in the night he is like a thief.” (Job 24:14) This is a dark verse, and Job doesn't soften it. He's naming the harm done to the poor and needy.

The answer is False. Job says, “In the dark they dig through houses; by day they shut themselves in, never to experience the light.” (Job 24:16) They don't come out into the light like everyone else. Job says the opposite, friends.

Job says their portion of the land is cursed. He says, “their portion of the land is cursed, so that no one turns toward their vineyards.” (Job 24:18) Their land is cursed, and no one turns toward their vineyards. That's quite a picture next to “…foam on the surface of the water…”

Job compares it to heat consuming melting snow. He says, “As drought and heat consume the melting snow, so Sheol steals those who have sinned.” (Job 24:19) Drought and heat consuming melting snow is the picture he uses for Sheol stealing those who have sinned. Snow doesn't stand a chance against drought and heat.

The answer is True. Job says, “The womb forgets them; the worm feeds on them; they are remembered no more.” (Job 24:20) It's a sober line about where those who have sinned end up. Job is not cheering here, friends. He's describing what he says happens.

What's really going on is that God's eyes are on their ways. Job says, “He gives them a sense of security, but His eyes are on their ways.” (Job 24:23) The mighty may feel safe. God is still watching every step. Feeling secure and being secure are two different things.

The word is “moment.” Job says, “They are exalted for a moment, then they are gone…” (Job 24:24) A moment is short. The mighty may look high up, but it doesn't last. They are brought low like all others.

Job dares anyone to prove him a liar. He says, “If this is not so, then who can prove me a liar and reduce my words to nothing?” (Job 24:25) He's standing behind everything he just said, friends. He's daring anyone to show him wrong.
